score_notes.novelty: Web Locks API (navigator.locks.request exclusive) is a fresh primitive the catalogue has never used, and its literal semantic — mutual exclusion across tabs — is exactly the readymade Benjamin critique has needed; only the web can do this.
score_notes.nuance: Mechanism and concept collapse into one object (the mutex IS the aura), and the work is double-coded without a wall text: a casual viewer sees a picture that vanishes when opened twice, a literate one sees aura reduced to a per-browser mutex — the joke that 'unique existence at the place where it happens to be' turns out to mean your laptop, this tab.
score_notes.narrative: Directly answers The Original (2026) which also took Benjamin as a target, but with a different mechanism (Blob + localStorage edition counter vs. Web Locks mutex); sits firmly on the order pole of the chance/order axis and adds 'concurrency primitives as material' to the twenty-year argument.
score_notes.craft: Lean build: inline canvas, a short script, a feature gate for browsers without the API, a 1Hz queue-refresh interval, a pagehide release; nothing decorative, nothing apologetic, and the gold-ground icon is the minimum the lock has to guard.
score_notes.wit: The joke and the mechanism are the same thing — a webpage you cannot open twice is funny precisely because the web's whole miracle is the costless simultaneous copy; the absurdity is the argument, the dry veil text lands it.

references_named: Walter Benjamin, The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction (1935)
rationale: All six hard gates pass: the work is web-native and could not exist as a print (G1), carries a real idea about aura and value (G2), makes the mechanism enact the concept (G3), is openly licensed with attribution and zero network or tracking (G4), reads in the cheerful-cynic voice (G5), and is materially distinct from the catalogue — Web Locks API has not been used before, and the only adjacent work (The Original) addresses the same Benjamin theme via a different primitive (G6). The novelty lies in the primitive itself: mutual exclusion across tabs is a genuine web-only affordance the catalogue had not touched, and it is precisely the affordance Benjamin's argument requires.
